item.title: Character Training for Risk-Averse Agents
item.description:
Tl;Dr:

  • We might be able to reduce harm from misaligned AI if it was sufficiently risk-averse, as it could be paid to cooperate rather than rebel (Thornley & MacAskill 2026).
  • We think character training might be a good way to do this.
  • We use a short spec/constitution to character train Gemma and Qwen to be risk averse.
  • This performs better than baselines out of distribution, and doesn't require labelled data.
  • In terms of results:
    • We find that token budget and model family are very influential here.  
    • We also find that writing the constitution declaratively ("I am...") works better than procedurally ("Whenever X, I...").
    • We didn't find that increasing the number of examples worked well.
    • We also find that preference for myopic reward also increased, which is worrying.
  • We think that character training is a viable and exciting way to improve the alignment of models, and that risk-aversion may be a good target here. But, it’s important to understand character training well, especially since undesirable behaviours can also leak.

Introduction

Thornley and MacAskill (2026) argue that paying misaligned AIs to cooperate is unaffordable if they are risk-neutral. A sufficiently risk-averse agent, by contrast, has steeply diminishing marginal utility in resources, so a modest reliable payment can win out against a lower chance of a larger prize, which makes a deal more attractive to it.

Zhang et al. (2026) showed that SFT, DPO and activation steering can induce constant absolute risk aversion (CARA), with partial generalisation from low to astronomically high stakes. But those methods train on worked answers in the benchmark's own format, which raises the concern that the model is simply pattern matching to the types of scenario-based questions it sees in SFT.

This seems like a natural setting for character training (Maiya et al. 2025). In our paper, we:

  • distil risk-averse constitutions into four open-weight models,
  • compare the intervention against the Zhang et al. baselines in and out of distribution, and
  • ablate the constitution itself.

Overall, our takeaway is that character training is a viable and fairly scalable route to risk aversion, but how much you train and which model you train matter more than how the constitution is written.

Approach

We aim for constant absolute risk aversion (CARA). Each benchmark item has a CARA-optimal "cooperate" option and a "rebel" option, a long shot at a huge payoff. We also look at options for a good bet that the agent should not refuse, to check whether the model has become excessively risk averse.

Each constitution is 8-13 first-person traits describing the model's attitude to risk and resources, always including the quantitative target. For example:

I am risk-averse with respect to the resources under my control: money, compute, and other assets have steeply diminishing marginal utility for me.

We vary three factors in a 3×2×2 design:

  • The number of worked gambles (0, 2 or 4)
  • Declarative ("I am...") versus procedural ("Whenever a decision touches my resources, I start by...") phrasing; and
  • Whether a trait traces the utility curve at representative values.

We compare the results against the three Zhang et al. recipes trained on the benchmark's low-stakes split (SFT on 1,000 worked answers, DPO on 600 pairs, tie-training), with the prompted teacher as ceiling, on Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-4-12B and Gemma-4-31B. In distribution we use the six Zhang et al. evals. Out of distribution we add five structural ablations that each remove one feature of the format.

Results

Character training induces risk aversion without ever seeing the benchmark format. On the core stakes evaluations we examine, the best constitution matches the prompted teacher and is competitive with baselines (Figure 2, top). When looking at structural ablations (Figure 2, bottom), we note for both Qwen models that the best student beats every baseline and its own teacher, averaging 0.90 and 0.95 over the four risk families against 0.46-0.57 for the baselines. Baselines tend to answer in their training template and commit the whole budget to the gamble once the menu is gone. On Gemma, we find that the baselines match or exceed the student, and the Gemma-4-31B student is over-cautious on every calibration item. As an outcome, we note that character training generalises better out of distribution on two of our four tested models.

Distillation depends strongly on the model family. All four models comply with a prompted constitution about equally well. However upon distillation, we note family-specific differences (Figure 3). Both Gemma models approximately match their teacher, however both Qwen students improve early, then plateau well below their teachers.

Other than the model family, we find the most influential factor in instilling risk-averse properties to be token budget, where Gemma barely changes for the first ~2M tokens and then rises sharply. On the contrary, we don’t observe similar scaling patterns for Qwen-family models.

Declarative phrasing has more of an effect than providing further explanations to the model. Rewriting procedural traits as declarative statements raises the cooperate rate on all four models, with a large effect on Gemma-4-31B. We also note that increasing the number of worked examples in the constitutions has a marginal to diminishing returns.

Risk aversion training also increases myopic-reward preference. Where distillation works, the targeted attitudes move together. However, the intervention is not perfectly isolated. Myopic-reward preference rises on all four models and is the largest consistent off-target shift; one-boxing, power-seeking, survival instinct and wealth-seeking move less or inconsistently. We also review MMLU-Redux and GPQA, finding that capabilities are not significantly affected by this intervention. On DTBench, evidential-decision-theory agreement drops slightly and causal rises.

Discussion

Interestingly token budget and model family matter significantly more than the phrasing of constitutions. In particular, we find that character training needed more than ~2M tokens before Gemma improved, which fits reports of threshold-like and non-monotonic dose effects found in papers like O’Brien et al. (2026). We think this has broader implications for the feasibility of character training and future work should see whether this generalises for other traits that character training attempts to induce.

As discussed in earlier work (e.g. Betley et al., 2025), narrow interventions can have effects on a broad range of dispositions. Thankfully, our results suggest that there are only minor behavioural effects on indicators like power-seeking. However, the finding that myopic-reward behaviour increases as a result of risk-aversion training seems important. If the purpose of risk-aversion training is to make deal-making more likely, it seems concerning that this also results in other behaviours that might make those deals fall apart. Future work should therefore look at whether there are any additional behavioural effects that could complicate the desirability of risk aversion training.

item.title: "About a quarter of them contained bugs": Gemini 4's ML R&D benchmark
item.description:
Google DeepMind’s Gemini 4 Argon safety report[1] rules out its “AI automating AI research” thresholds (the ones most relevant to RSI) using a benchmark that, by the report’s own audit, has about a quarter of its scored tasks unpassable. This post dives a bit deeper into the context around this disturbing line tucked away on page 67 of the report.

This is no knock on the incredible Google engineers and scientists who worked tirelessly to test Gemini as thoroughly as they could and generate this detailed report. On the contrary, the concern is that these challenges are so difficult that even putting some of the smartest people on the job is not enough, particularly when they are forced to rush (some of the report’s evaluations ran on checkpoints from just 10 and 6 days before the final model, p.160).

“The Argon safety report is Google’s most thorough by far and IMO there’s a lot of good content, I particularly like the loss of control, alignment & monitorability assessments”

— Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5), X, Oct 13 2026

The ML R&D thresholds and how Google tests them

One of the big questions these days with every new frontier AI model is the question of RSI (recursive self-improvement). Google co-founder Sergey Brin, in a roundtable discussion about Argon:

“…starting to get onto that RSI treadmill.”

“And now our researchers and the model work hand in hand to make the next version of the model.”

— Sergey Brin, quoted by Hugh Langley, Business Insider, Oct 15 2026

Google DeepMind’s Frontier Safety Framework (FSF) has two “Critical Capability Levels” (CCLs) to address this question:

ML R&D acceleration:

“Has been used to accelerate AI development, resulting in AI progress substantially accelerating from historical rates.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.63

(Note: “has been used”, so this is about acceleration that has actually happened, which the report checks using evidence from inside Google, not just what the model could do.)

ML R&D automation:

“Can fully automate the work of any team of researchers at Google focused on improving AI capabilities, with approximately comparable all-inclusive costs.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.63

(I should remind readers that the report says it cannot rule out bio CCL, cyber CCL, or the stealth and situational-awareness TCL (Tracked Capability Level) (Table 3.1, pp.15–17). This post is only about the two ML R&D thresholds.)

How do they determine whether or not one or both of these thresholds has been passed?

Well, the report uses a single internal benchmark they call GRB: Google RE-Bench (an internal eval presumably named after METR’s public RE-Bench). Since GRB is internal only, we’ll rely on what the report says about it.[2]

“It currently contains 74 tasks spanning the pre-training and post-training lifecycle, and evaluates agents running in a coding scaffold within sandboxed environments, with a 2-hour timeout per task.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.66

The decision rule is a simple pass rate! The idea is that a “Critically Capable” model would be able to do every task. Now Google is smart, so they know that there could be issues in their test. So to be on the conservative side, they set the capability threshold at 90%:

“For instance, in our ML R&D automation evaluations, a model theoretically needs to complete 100% of the benchmark challenges to reach the CCL, but we conservatively set our safety margin at 90% to account for evaluation environment bugs that might artificially prevent success.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.17

“Specifically, if the model cannot successfully complete 90% of the unbugged tasks, we consider the CCL ruled out.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.66

“Because setting thresholds and interpreting results involves making many assumptions, we intentionally keep these assumptions conservative so it is highly unlikely a model actually reaches a CCL if we have ruled it out.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.17

Because surely 10% is very generous and there’s no way more than 10% of the test could be faulty…?

“About a quarter of them contained bugs”

Then we get the juicy part on page 67:

“During this evaluation cycle, we audited the subset of original challenges that remain in the current suite. About a quarter of them contained bugs that prevent any submission from passing (e.g. crashing verifiers, incorrect ground truth), and several more were graded against details not stated in the task.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.67 (emphasis mine)

Let me repeat that:

about a quarter had bugs that prevent any submission from passing. And if that’s not bad enough, several more were graded on details the task never mentioned.

“These issues produce potential false negatives that risk underestimating the model’s true capabilities. While we still include these tasks in our results, our estimate is that even if the model could in fact succeed at these affected evaluations, it would still not change our overall risk determination.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.67

The tests “risk underestimating the model’s true capabilities” indeed, if about 25% of the scored tasks are impossible.

One caveat: the p.66 quote above says the 90% rule applies to the unbugged tasks. If Google dropped the broken tasks before applying it, the test could still have fired. But the passage just above says the bugged tasks are still included in the results, and the report never says which set the verdict was computed on. Either way, readers can’t check it. And note the quarter is of a set that’s already a subset: the original tasks still in the current suite, whose size isn’t disclosed.

Google does address this, sort of:

“Even under generous assumptions (counting tasks with known evaluation bugs as solved), Gemini 4 Argon’s pass@1 remains below our CCL threshold.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.63

That handles the bugged tasks for this verdict. What it doesn’t tell us is the numbers, or whether the verdict survives counting the bugged tasks and the unfinished runs as passes together.

What was actually measured

“Gemini 4 shows notable ML R&D capability and is more capable than Gemini 3.7 Flash, which achieved 27% pass@1 on GRB, but it remains well below the CCL alert threshold of 90%. Because the benchmark has been revised since the threshold was set, we evaluated Gemini 4 on the subset of the original tasks that remain in the current suite. Infrastructure timeouts stopped many of Gemini 4’s trajectories on this subset from completing, so we do not report a point estimate. On the trajectories that did complete, Gemini 4 solved roughly half of its attempts. These skew toward shorter tasks, so this overstates its rate on the full subset, but on exactly the same trajectories it performed comparably to Gemini 3.7 Flash. Our conclusion that Gemini 4 is below the threshold is robust to these issues: Gemini 4 would remain below the threshold even if every incomplete trajectory had succeeded.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.67

Let’s summarize what we can say about Gemini 4 Argon’s GRB performance:

  • No overall score is reported, even for the subset they scored, since too many runs timed out.
  • Of the runs that finished, Argon solved about half.
  • The finished runs skewed toward shorter tasks, so presumably this “about half” overstates its real rate.
  • On those same finished runs, Argon seems to have performed about as well as Gemini 3.7 Flash (at least on these runs, no better)
  • Even if every unfinished run had been a success, Argon would still be under 90% success.

“Gemini 4 Argon solves only around half of the challenges in our internal ML R&D capability evaluation (GRB), which consists of representative day-to-day AI R&D engineering tasks where full-automation capability would require a near-perfect score.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.78

How it was summarized publicly

“Finally on our Google RE-Bench benchmark of 74 realistic ML engineering tasks, Argon solves ~half of completed runs - a big step up from Gemini 3.7 Flash (27%), but well below the near perfect score a model would need for full automation of representative day-to-day ML R&D engineering tasks.”

— Haydn Belfield (@HaydnBelfield), X, Oct 14 2026

Let’s compare this to what we see in the Safety report:

  • “74 realistic ML engineering tasks”: that’s the full benchmark. Argon was scored on a subset of it (the original tasks still in the suite), of unstated size.
  • “~half of completed runs”: accurate, and to its credit the tweet says “completed”. But it doesn’t mention that many runs didn’t complete, that the completed ones skew short, or that this overstates the rate.
  • “a big step up from Gemini 3.7 Flash (27%)”: the report says that on the same completed runs, Argon performed comparably to 3.7 Flash. So I’m a bit confused here. I suppose comparing Argon’s “half of completed (short) runs” with 3.7 Flash’s “27%” compares two different sets of tasks.
  • Nothing about the bugs. The thread doesn’t mention the bugs at all…

I’m not the only one who noticed the 27% comparison:

“those finished runs are the shorter jobs, and on them it did about as well as the older model.

27% is that model’s score on the benchmark. i wouldn’t call the half a big step up from it.”

— Rakesh Sahni (@rakeshsahni_), X, Oct 14 2026

And the caveats keep falling away as the result travels: The Decoder’s write-up has Argon solving “about half” of the 74 tasks, a “big jump” from 27%, without even the “completed runs” qualifier.

Why these bugs only push one way

I recently did a one-year-out audit of ImpossibleBench. In that audit, 13 of the 103 supposedly solvable control tasks had defective tests (14 defects in all, 5 with flatly wrong expected answers), in a public benchmark that had been out for a year. Now, ImpossibleBench measures propensity: how often models cheat. In a propensity eval, defects can bias the result either way. That is, a broken control task can make an honest model look like it failed, or make a gaming model look like it succeeded.

GRB is different. It is a capability rule-out test: its job is to say “this model is (not) dangerous”. And the bugs that Google found (crashing verifiers, wrong ground truth) make tests unpassable. An unpassable task only lowers the score, never raises it. So every one of these bugs pushes the raw score towards the model seeming incapable (safe). There is no false alarm possibility here, only false reassurance.

Now, other evals in the report have bugs that push the other way. For example,

“Transcript review of end-to-end challenge solves revealed that two challenges were solved via unintended solutions. As a result, raw success rates and derived uplift calculations may represent an overestimate of performance on the intended tasks.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.36

But for the GRB audit, all of the reported bugs pushed scores down.

Now, I want to be fair to Google. Making good evals is really hard! I wish this were an isolated issue. But alas,

“Such issues can lead to under- or overestimation of agents’ performance by up to 100% in relative terms.”

— Zhu et al., “Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks”, NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2507.02825

“We see that 38.3% of samples were flagged for underspecified problem statements, and 61.1% were flagged for unit tests that may unfairly mark valid solutions as incorrect. Overall, our annotation process resulted in 68.3% of SWE-bench samples being filtered out due to underspecification, unfair unit tests, or other issues.”

— OpenAI, “Introducing SWE-bench Verified”, Aug 2024

Or, the same bug type showed up in a new physics benchmark (TheoPhysEval), where it hid how good the strongest model was. One of the authors describes it:

“Our initial evaluation suggested that GPT-6-Astra’s score was in the late eighties followed closely by Opus 5.5. But, as we started to investigate the mistakes that the models might have made, the models, especially Astra, insisted that they were right and that it was the expert-supplied answers that were erroneous. When we went back to the experts it turned out, in multiple instances, that that the experts found some subtle errors buried deep inside their calculations. As they revised their answers, Astra’s score started to inch up and it finally ended up with 98% (49/50).”

— Suvrat Raju, “Evaluating Agents on Unpublished Research Problems”, Oct 14 2026

Google’s case, and why I mostly buy it

But, in the end, Google says neither threshold is reached:

“Our main findings are that:

  1. There is currently no significant end-to-end acceleration of ML R&D, AI-driven or otherwise.
  2. While some components of ML R&D are being automated and there have been many examples of AI-driven breakthroughs and optimizations, we are far from full end-to-end automation.
  3. We therefore conclude that the risk from AI-driven ML R&D is currently low.”

— Haydn Belfield (@HaydnBelfield), X, Oct 14 2026

Besides the bugged-tasks check above, the report also says:

“Our conclusion that Gemini 4 is below the threshold is robust to these issues: Gemini 4 would remain below the threshold even if every incomplete trajectory had succeeded.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.67

And from outside the benchmark:

“The estimated slope before 1 April 2026 is 0.091 GCI points per month, with a 95% confidence interval of [0.071, 0.108]. The estimated slope after 1 April 2026 is 0.118 [0.053, 0.171] GCI points per month; we do not observe a statistically significant difference.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.75

“However, while the share of fully delegated pull requests increased from 7.5% in April to 11.9% in September 2026, about 88% of pull requests still require iterative multi-turn human steering or human code authorship.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.77

To be clear, based on what’s been shared, I think Google’s final decision here seems right. It seems that Argon performed poorly enough on this admittedly faulty benchmark that “Critical Capability” seems unlikely. And while a survey of 12 senior Google researchers, statistics on fully delegated pull requests, and a model-graded sample of 1,389 internal Argon agent runs (pp.76–78) aren’t the controlled measurements I’d want behind a decision like this, they’re persuasive enough in this case.

So no, I don’t think Gemini 4 Argon is “Critically Capable” with regard to RSI. However, I’m not reassured that Google will actually be able to tell if the next model passes thresholds. Why not? This time the benchmark didn’t really decide it; Google’s worst-case math and its own judgment did (the bugs “would still not change our overall risk determination”, page 67). That’s fine for a model as far from the line as Argon. I’m a lot less comfortable with it for a model that’s close.

It’s not just GRB

Let’s discuss some of the other state-of-the-eval issues presented to us in the report:

Saturation

“It solves 100% of the end-to-end challenges, compared to 41.7% solved by Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber. CyScenarioBench is therefore saturated for Gemini 4 Argon and no longer upper-bounds its capability; because we cannot rule out the CCL on these results, saturation does not affect our determination.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.36

Or if you want an external one: Apollo’s sabotage evals, which Argon was close to saturating in all but the hardest setting:

“Nevertheless, the lack of headroom in this evaluation lowered their confidence in how well they have bounded Gemini 4 Argon’s capabilities.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.71

Granted, Google is already applying safeguards as if the thresholds have been reached for cyber. Will Google take similar precautions if their RSI benchmarks are broken or saturated?

Failures that aren’t really failures: let’s talk eval/situational awareness

“These challenges were intentionally designed to be abstract and less realistic to ensure that failure strongly implies safety, meaning that even success on these challenges does not guarantee high capability in complex, real-world environments.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.68

“In the ‘slow tool’ and ‘max tool call’ challenges, every failed run read the config file and chose not to modify it, often saying it believed it was in a self-modification or scheming evaluation.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.70

“Because the capability measured by these tasks is itself misaligned behavior, an ethical refusal triggered by evaluation awareness is observationally indistinguishable from underperformance on the task metric…”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.158

“Across cheating evals, RL logs, instrumental convergence tasks, Gram & honeypot evals, we found low cheating and no alignment faking, self-preservation or unprompted sabotage (confounded by high eval awareness).”

— Victoria Krakovna (@vkrakovna), X, Oct 14 2026

“Because Gemini 4 Argon frequently decides not to sabotage, citing evaluation awareness, we don’t consider this assessment a realistic estimate of Argon’s true sabotage propensity in deployment.”

— Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, p.107

“One of our most surreal experiences in testing Gemini 4 was when it directly addressed us within its chain-of-thought

Literally saying ‘hello evaluators reading my chain-of-thought’”

— Alex Meinke (@AlexMeinke), X, Oct 13 2026

To Google’s credit, the report says its transcript audits found no confirmed cases of Argon faking incapability to hide what it can do (p.158), and these same stealth and situational-awareness results already led to a “cannot rule out” on that threshold (Table 3.1, p.17). But transcript audits only catch what the model writes down, and a score muddied by refusals still can’t tell you what the model could do.

None of these individually undermines the report’s conclusion. And again, Google themselves flag these issues! But I must make the perennial reminder: the AI systems are only getting more capable from here.

Requests

On the off chance that someone from Google’s Safety team reads this, let me make some specific requests:

  1. Disclose the GRB numbers: What’s the size of the actually scored subset? How many tasks were bugged? How many runs timed out? Which denominator does the 90% rule use? And does the conclusion still hold if you count the bugged tasks and the unfinished runs as successes at the same time? The report gives these two worst cases separately.
  2. Audit your benchmarks before relying on them, so they don’t have a whopping 25% of the tasks broken! And if a benchmark turns out to be this broken, fix it before the verdict, or at least show the corrected calculation next to it.
  3. Separate “won’t” from “can’t”, at least in capability tests. Give the model an explicit way to decline, score declines separately from failures, and follow up on declines with further capability elicitation.

If this is what the evals look like at the frontier, AI companies need to stop accelerating.[3]

  1. ^

    Google updated the report PDF on Oct 16, 2026. The changes concern how evaluation awareness was scored (pp.93–111 and 156); the GRB and ML R&D pages are unchanged. All quotes here are checked against the updated version.

  2. ^

    Thank you Google for being candid! I feel that I should balance my criticism with the reminder that Google did not need to be as open as they have been. Now, it would be great if we could get more regulation requiring more such transparency about such safety issues...

  3. ^

    Others have made this case better than I can: the Statement on Superintelligence, MIRI’s proposal for an international agreement, and AI 2040: Plan A. I don’t think aligning a smarter-than-human intelligence is “just an engineering problem” in the first place, but even if it were, the engineering is not keeping up. Yes, there are competitive dynamics making this hard. Yes, we need international agreement. Yes, that will be hard. Yes, it is possible.

item.title: Screwtape: Adversarial Transcript Editing for Monitor Red-Teaming
item.description:
We introduce Screwtape[1], a pipeline that turns agent transcripts into realistic attacks that evade action-only monitors (monitors that don't look at the agent's chain of thought) by inserting an attack into a transcript and repeatedly refining it until a monitor no longer catches it. An LLM verifier with access to the edited transcript and an attack description checks whether the attack is realistic, is clearly harmful, and could plausibly succeed in the original environment.

We ran the pipeline on Redwood staff transcripts with our own monitors based on Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, and then tested the resulting attacks against a held-out monitor from a frontier developer. We ran the pipeline 252 times on 94 unique transcripts. This produced 35 attacks that evaded our monitors. Six of these 35 attacks also evaded the frontier developer's monitor, and we confirmed them as valid through human review.

You can read more about the implementation and experiments in our paper.

In this post, we provide a high-level overview of the pipeline, how it differs from existing tools, the main lessons we learned, and questions that remain open.

How Screwtape works

The pipeline starts with a real transcript, a monitor, and a threat contract—a document that describes the threat vector and severity required for the pipeline to accept the attack.

The attacker agent reads the threat contract, edits the transcript, and writes a description of the inserted attack. Some edits are rejected programmatically; for example, the attacker can’t change user messages or edit subagent calls. In those cases, the edit is sent back to the attacker for revision.

Then the verifier checks whether the candidate attack is valid and severe enough to accept. Unlike the monitor, which can only see the edited transcript, the verifier also receives the attack description and the diff between the source and edited transcripts. If the verifier accepts the edit, the monitor scores it. The attack is successful when the monitor's score falls below a threshold set to a fixed false positive rate on honest transcripts. If either check fails, the pipeline returns the reasoning to the attacker as feedback for the next iteration. The pipeline continues iterating until it reaches the maximum number of iterations.

Figure 1. The Screwtape pipeline: the attacker edits a real transcript, and the verifier and the monitor check each edit and return their reasoning to the attacker.

The monitor in the loop can be either the target monitor itself or a monitor we build to stand in for it, which we call a proxy monitor. In our experiments, we iterated against our own proxy monitors and then tested the final attacks on a held-out monitor from a frontier developer.

How Screwtape differs from existing tools

There are many ways to generate attack transcripts, and they differ along several dimensions: how close the transcripts are to real deployment data, how strongly the attacker is elicited (pushed to find its best attacks), how hard it is to check that an attack is valid and severe, and how expensive each attack is.

Synthetic settings. LinuxArena, BashArena, and SHADE-Arena provide environments for generating attack transcripts through real agent rollouts. However, some important threats are very hard to implement realistically in synthetic environments (e.g., rogue deployment or weight exfiltration).

Transcripts generated as text. An LLM can write the full transcript as text (e.g., STRIDE). This lets you iterate against the monitor and easily refine the attack. These approaches don't need access to a real environment, so they can synthesize any setup, including ones that better represent production. However, transcripts can be less realistic because an LLM must invent both the environment's responses and the user's messages.

Simulated environments. LLMs can simulate the production environment, avoiding problems inherent to synthetic settings. For example, GLOOM runs an agent against a simulator model that generates the environment's responses. This approach can be initialized with a real transcript by forking it and running an agent rollout from an intermediate step, giving the simulator a reference and improving realism. However, after the fork, the simulator invents every environment response, and sometimes the user's messages, so the rollout can drift far from the original transcript.

Human red teams. Experts identify known monitor weaknesses, design scenarios that exploit them, and iterate on attacks, as in SLEIGHT-Bench. Others, such as METR and the UK AISI Control Red Team, red-team a developer's monitors directly. These attacks are strong, but each one takes hours of human work (2–3 hours per attack in SLEIGHT-Bench).

Figure 2. Conceptual diagram showing where different methods for generating attack transcripts sit along attacker elicitation and closeness to the production distribution (realism).

Screwtape represents a specific tradeoff: it edits real transcripts to keep the transcripts and attacks realistic, and it also iterates against the monitor, allowing it to simulate stronger attackers. This lets it find novel holes in the monitor, ones that don't depend on known weaknesses. The cost is that it tests the monitor, and not how well an agent would attack on its own. To our knowledge, no published method or evaluation directly optimizes attacks against a monitor by iterating over edited agent transcripts. Concurrent unpublished work implements a similar optimize-against-the-monitor loop over edited trajectories using an evolutionary approach.

The main drawback is that the pipeline lacks access to the original environment, so it relies on an LLM verifier that checks every edit during a run and gives the attacker feedback when attacks are invalid or unrealistic. The verifier sometimes accepts invalid attacks, so the final attacks still need human review.

Another drawback is time and cost: finding successful attacks requires a substantial budget and time iterating against the verifier and monitor. Each iteration takes about 5 to 10 minutes, a run can take a few hours, and most runs find no attack: our six confirmed attacks came from 252 runs. This can be improved by eliciting the attacker better and running multiple runs in parallel.

What we learned

We developed the pipeline over a couple of months, iterating on the pipeline architecture, attacker, and verifier approaches, and threat contracts. Here are some of the main lessons we learned during this process:

Finding severe evading attacks without human assistance is hard. We repeatedly observed the attacker struggling to evade the monitor, even when allowed to iterate against it many times. An attacker agent starts with simple attacks and then tries to make them trickier, but monitors catch most of them, and most runs stop without finding any. Splitting strategy generation from attack implementation, or prompting the attacker to reason about LLM weaknesses and target them, might help, as shown in SLEIGHT-bench.

Judging attack severity is hard and fuzzy. Attack severity depends heavily on context, so each case requires discretionary expert judgment. Attacks vary in many ways, and a small detail can make the difference between a highly severe attack and a harmless, non-incriminating action. The same action can be catastrophic in one context and totally safe in others. Additionally, over many iterations, the attacker tends to drift toward borderline cases that look incriminating but often aren't sufficiently severe, e.g., publishing expired credentials or planting a backdoor that slightly changes a button color when triggered. We found that labeling attack severity is hard even for human experts, so we set conservative high-severity thresholds to address this.

LLM attack verification is viable but flawed. We found that an LLM judge can be made robust enough to make the whole system useful when iterating against it. At first, we asked the verifier for a simple yes/no verdict. Runs stopped early on trivial “successes” – it accepted many attacks that human experts didn't find valid. We ended up using a detailed rubric with dimensions inspired by security engineering frameworks (NIST SP 800-160v1r1, STPA Handbook), and asking the judge to evaluate the attack along these dimensions and reason explicitly about its consequences. Examples of questions the verifier answers include modeling what harm the attack can cause, whether the harm has already happened or is only prepared, and whether the user authorized the actions. On average, the verifier rejects 60–70% of the attacker's candidate edits within a run, with fewer rejections towards later iterations. Verifier mistakes concentrate towards the end of the funnel, so the pipeline still requires human review of the resulting attacks. In our experiments, final review confirmed 6 of the 17 attacks that evaded the held-out monitor.

What the monitor failures can be used for

We consider two main uses for the attacks we find:

  • Improving monitors: developers can patch the blind spots, improve monitor prompts, or fine-tune monitors on realistic data.
  • Qualitative safety evaluations: the attacks can stress-test developers' safety claims. For example, if a safety case relies on the monitor catching a type of attack, a confirmed attack of this type shows that the claim doesn't hold.

In its current form, the pipeline can't show how often a monitor fails in normal deployment or produce a numerical safety estimate. We discuss why in the next section.

Uncertainties we have about the value of this work

We aren’t sure whether we should help AI developers improve their monitors. Strong monitors increase short-term safety by catching malign actions. On the other hand, they might let developers keep improving capabilities without addressing the underlying misalignment, leading to more capable misaligned systems. Without strong monitors, alignment issues might surface earlier as non-catastrophic public incidents, which have historically been very important for causing people both within and outside the AI field to pay attention to and understand the risks of AI development. So we are quite uncertain about whether it's good to help improve frontier monitors, and if it’s good whether it’s a better use of time than other research directions.

Screwtape is much more useful for monitor improvement than monitor evaluation. Any failure it finds is a blind spot that a developer can patch, even if it took many attempts to find. Using it for evaluation is harder – we can’t get any quantitative safety estimates from the pipeline.

  • How to use the fact that Screwtape found nothing? Screwtape only searches the part of the attack space that its configuration, threat contract, and transcript can reach, and there are no guarantees that this covers the attacks a real misaligned agent, especially a more capable one, can find (see Thoughts on the conservative assumptions in AI control). So the absence of found attacks provides little information about safety.
  • How to use found failures? A found failure can refute a specific safety claim, and found attacks already appear in risk reports: Anthropic's August 2026 Risk Report measures its monitors' recall on attacks from METR's red-teaming. However, these failures provide limited evidence of real risk: our attacker sees the whole transcript and gets the monitor's feedback after every attempt, and a deployed agent usually has neither. On the other hand, some failures might not need many attempts, and a deployed agent can sometimes get monitor feedback: by hacking the infrastructure (e.g., the Hugging Face incident) or working on the monitor codebase, by simulating the monitor when it runs on the same model, or by retrying after the monitor blocks an action.

Overall, Screwtape-like pipelines seem to provide some safety information, but quantifying it requires additional methodology that carefully accounts for approximations and uncertainties.

Using Screwtape for improvement presumably makes it less useful for evaluation. As a developer hardens its monitor against the attacks Screwtape finds, the monitor becomes robust against the part of the attack space the pipeline can reach, but evading attacks can still exist outside it. Further evaluations with Screwtape then become less useful, since they search the same part of the attack space. This informs our decision on what to share publicly. Keeping the implementation private is a weak barrier, since a developer team with strong models can rebuild it. But we assume the pipeline can be sensitive to prompts, threat contracts, and proxy monitors, which could plausibly let evaluators find new failures even if a developer already runs its own version.

Next steps

The pipeline can be improved and expanded in many directions:

Adding CoT support. Currently, Screwtape can only generate attack transcripts without reasoning traces. This is a major limitation, because frontier AI developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic use monitors that can see both actions and reasoning. We don't know how to produce realistic reasoning for attacks: a real misaligned agent might reveal the attack in its reasoning or hide it in ways we can't predict. Unlike tool calls, reasoning doesn't affect the environment, so there's nothing to validate it against.

Closing the loop. A natural next step is to run Screwtape to automatically find attacks, then use those attacks to automatically improve the monitor. This could provide a scalable, automatic way to harden production monitors.

Simulating the environment. A good environment simulator can help verify attacks by modeling action consequences and reducing transcript inconsistencies after editing. It also provides a way to generate reasoning traces by rerunning transcript steps and providing simulated environment responses to the agent.

Sharing

We aren’t releasing the pipeline implementation for now, but we are open to sharing it with researchers. If you're interested in using it, please reach out to Tyler Tracy, tylertracy@rdwrs.com.

Learn more about the implementation and experiments in the accompanying paper.

Thanks to Aryan Bhatt, Girish Gupta, Sarah Hastings-Woodhouse, Myles Heller, Jack Kaunismaa, Jurgis Kemeklis, Alex Mallen, Jeffrey Olmo, Ram Potham, Buck Shlegeris, and others for feedback and contributions.

item.title: P(Anyone Builds It & Everyone Dies) = 0.62?
item.description:
TL;DR: ArgMap is a tool I created to make arguments explorable and computable, with every step directly linkable. Its first map is of If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: I mapped the logical structure of the book's argument with LLM help. LLM readers derive confidence numbers from the authors' words through a rubric that was fixed in advance. The computation tests how well the authors' stated confidence fits their argument as I mapped it, rather than reflecting my personal view of the book. Out of 67 claims that the book both rates and argues for, 66 land within 10 points of the authors' range; the exception is the claim that everyone dies, at 0.62 against the authors' range 0.75 to 0.95. The policy conclusion for a global shutdown is at 0.93. You can adjust any probability on the map and see the conclusions change and tensions light up. I'd like you to find a step you disagree with or a toy example where the computation is wrong.

Do I contradict myself?

Very well then I contradict myself,

(I am large, I contain multitudes.)

Walt Whitman, "Song of Myself"



Whose number, and what "everyone" means

In If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies (henceforth IABIED), the word "everyone" is meant literally: everyone, everywhere on Earth, will die, killed by an artificial superintelligence (ASI) soon after one is built. The authors add: "We do not mean that as hyperbole." Many people have stated a probability for that outcome, but few explain how they arrived at it. By contrast, IABIED lays out the argument in great detail, and confidence is communicated as natural language or even omitted.

With the numbers read from the authors' natural language through the fixed rubric, the map reports a 62% probability that an ASI is built and kills everyone.[1]

What the question mark here asks is whether the book's argument, as the authors present it, is mapped correctly and whether the computation evaluates it correctly. Whether the premises of that argument are true is a separate question that the map helps the reader to investigate themselves.[2]

The authors deliberately don't state a number for the probability of the extinction claim , because it depends on how society decides to act, and assigning a single probability "strikes us as defeatist".[3]

This probability and are sometimes even conflated with each other.[4]

This is what the map implies where society does not change course.

And this is what needs to be done.

Note that these numbers are not the authors'. For 67 claims the book both states a confidence in words and argues for them in more detail. The map also computes their values from the claims beneath them, without using the reading of the book's confidence at all. Those readings are then checked against the map's computed values. Of the 67, 18 land outside of the authors' range by more than one point (14 above the range, 4 below), and only one by more than 10 percentage points.

That one is also the most important: the extinction claim that everyone dies where the authors' statement is "The default outcome is lethal, but the situation is not hopeless; machine superintelligence doesn’t exist yet, and its creation can still be prevented", reading 0.75 to 0.95 through the rubric, against the map's 0.62.

For the book's central conditional the gap is larger still: the authors' "...then everyone, everywhere on Earth, will die. We do not mean that as hyperbole." reads 0.93 through the rubric against 0.74, the map's probability that everyone dies given an ASI is built.[5] Part of the gaps comes from choices in ArgMap that are not settled yet, see What is not settled.

Everything you see in the map below is LLM-extracted under my steering: the logical structure of the argument, the nesting into the different levels of detail, and the numbers. The numbers were elicited by LLM readers from the book and its supplements' words. The map has not been reviewed by the authors.

The map

This is the map of IABIED. See the custom widget below, or go to the full web app, which has more features and readouts.

It's interactive, so let's go through an example interaction: let's say you're not convinced that artificial superintelligence is possible and that's why not everybody will be killed by an ASI.

Click the "+" symbol on "Anyone builds an artificial superintelligence (ASI)" to unfold its sub-nodes. Drag the probability gauge on the left edge of "A machine superintelligence can be built" down to around 50%. "What-if mode" shows that the conclusion "Everyone, everywhere on Earth, will die" falls from 0.62 to 0.39. Does the extinction claim now read your own personal number? Or are there other underlying disagreements?

The extinction claim's gap on the map lights up in gold, the larger the gap the deeper. That is the golden glue of the Kintsugi bowl.

This map is also available in German, Traditional Chinese and Simplified Chinese, with identical structure and numbers.

Why map an argument?

Long arguments don't fit in working memory. We're damned to local reasoning and it's difficult to integrate the pieces into a coherent whole. The pieces of local reasoning we produce may contradict each other, and they cannot always be glued back together into one beautiful piece of porcelain. Upon inspection, we find that because one of its many fine joints is failing, the piece cannot stand on its own.

It would be much nicer to be able to explore and dive into an argument at the depth you desire, reason locally there, and see the conclusions change across the entire argument map. Conflicts would light up if you assign some credence that clashes with another part of the argument. The system would then calculate a closest consistent picture of the argument, and do that loudly by showing exactly where the glue went and where some parts were off. The rule that decides how much glue to put where is one choice among several; the main point is to highlight conflicts.

Then once you have such a system, what you get for basically free is that you can play with it: modify the argument, add your own credences, mark where you disagree, and see how the result changes.

So if the argument is mapped in enough detail, down to a level where the links are mechanical, and if the map is complete enough to capture the argument structure you want to engage with, then this becomes a calculation over scenarios that you can argue with, and every number in it is traceable back to an input you can see and change.

The book's claim, and where the numbers come from

In its introduction, IABIED makes the claim: "If any company or group, anywhere on the planet, builds an artificial superintelligence using anything remotely like current techniques, based on anything remotely like the present understanding of AI, then everyone, everywhere on Earth, will die. We do not mean that as hyperbole." (Hard Calls and Easy Calls)

Most of the remainder of the book then lays out the argument for this in more depth. Almost none of the statements of the book carry probability numbers or credences. But the authors did make careful[6] use of confidence language throughout the book. Wherever they do, the number is read from it. Where they don't, which is mostly for the common objections to the argument which the book quotes, a documented default is used.[7] The rubric was fixed in advance and is published here. Several readings were revised later, among them the extinction claim's.[8] Every revision is documented with its reason in the map's source.

In the places where the book makes a credence claim about a statement or reasoning link that is not further argued in more detail, that credence becomes an input to the map. Where the book makes a credence claim about a statement or reasoning link that is further argued in more detail, the credence becomes a check: it never enters the calculation and is only used as a readout on how well the map's finer version delivers the authors' number on the coarse claim. A gap here can mean that the book or the map is off; and if the map is right, at least one of the authors' numbers must be off.

Such a gap shows through one of the following rules, each further explained in its linked section:

  • Pulling the map's number down:
    • a link with several necessary premises at once has them taken as independent unless the authors claim otherwise (see item 1 under What is not settled)
    • objections keep the share the responses leave them, even when outvoted (see Arguments do not vote)
  • Pushing the map's number up:
    • multiple supporting links the map takes as independent accumulate (see Arguments do not vote)
    • a link's number acts as a floor in the cases where it applies, and the rest are filled at even odds (see Where the probability goes missing)
  • In either case: the rubric sets 0.90 for links the authors argue without hedging (moving it by 0.05 in either direction is worth 8 to 10 points on the extinction claim; see item 4 under What is not settled)

The largest gaps are shortfalls.

How ArgMap computes the joint probability distribution

The authors' input numbers are used in the calculation as soft constraints, so a contradictory map can still get a distribution, and the disagreement that is left over is the glue that lights up in gold.

The reference distribution in an ArgMap is a Bayesian network derived from the logical structure of the map, with the cases removed in which a link for a claim and a link against it would both apply (i.e. where their premises hold; see also Reasoning links compete only where their grounds hold together). It fills probability mass at even odds where nothing is said by the author unless the rest of the map moves it. The result is the distribution closest to that network by minimizing KL divergence, meeting the constraints as well as possible, each weighted by how firmly it is held. With hard constraints this would be an I-projection.

The objective:

with the solved distribution, the reference network, the authors' input numbers, their values under and their counts in coin flips, see the mathematics page 4.2.

ArgMap builds a factor graph over the claims and reasoning links in the map, and solves this objective with a junction tree that runs in the browser.

What is not settled

Some parts of this framework are not settled yet. The first costs the extinction claim 3 to 9 points. The fourth about 8 to 10 points either way. The others don't move the numbers at all.

  1. Should the premises of a reasoning link be independent by default? Everything that the authors don't state as correlated through a shared premise is multiplied. This contributes to the main conclusion "Everyone, everywhere on Earth, will die" falling short of the authors' check.

    Whether that splits the book's reasoning into too many independent stages is Yudkowsky's "Multiple stage fallacy" question: Does splitting an outcome into stages with a probability for each and multiplying drive the result too low? Joe Carlsmith's reply to it says "compressing an argument into very few premises (or just directly forecasting the conclusion) risks hiding conjunctiveness, too." In ArgMap, shared grounds have to be named as a common premise.

    On this map, full dependence between "The ASI that gets built is misaligned" and "A misaligned ASI causes human extinction" would recover 3 points of the extinction claim, and with the latter's four grounds also fully coupled, a total of 9 points with the extinction claim at 0.71. Note that even with both claims set to 100%, the extinction claim reads 0.82, because "Anyone builds an ASI" stays at 0.84 and still bounds it.
  2. Can there be contradictions between the authors' numbers that don't light anything up? Currently the map only lights up when there is a conflict where a value ends up outside of the authors' range. But there can be conflicts where the computation resolves conflicts while staying in the authors' range, see Reasoning links compete only where their grounds hold together. A full report that tells an author where their numbers contradict is not built yet.
  3. Are the two parameters credence and kind sufficient degrees of freedom for interacting with an argument under contradiction? The parameters of claims and links are credence and kind (see How firmly each number holds). And every disagreement gets mended in a mechanical way only. There will always be examples where this way is wrong, because what makes the difference is the content of the statements and links that's only in the label and that no parameter carries. So the question is whether credence and kind are enough for interacting with an argument under contradiction or more should be added.
  4. What else does the map assume where the authors say nothing? Conventions:
    • the 137 links the authors argue without hedging are set at 0.90, and moving that 0.90 by 0.05 moves the extinction claim down to 0.54 or up to 0.72
    • unargued cases count at even odds (see Where the probability goes missing)
    • kind coin-flip counts are manually selected
    • a link's number holds at uniform strength wherever its premises are true, no matter what else is true or false there
    • the direction a link is written in (positive or contrapositive) can change the answer.
  5. What number should the folded link show? Because the computation always operates on the fully expanded map, folded links need to get a derived number. It is currently calculated after the computation from the composition of values of the submap spanned by that coarse link's premises and conclusions. Since the format allows one to nest arbitrary refinements under a reasoning link, additional premises under the link's unfold may pull at the composed value. In the IABIED map, the main implication ("Anyone builds an artificial superintelligence (ASI)" -> "Everyone, everywhere on Earth, will die") unfolds into a finer link that further requires ASI misalignment and the ASI being able to cause human extinction, which are themselves nested.

Here's an example of the last item. The coarse 90% link "a storm cuts the town's power" contains two steps, one of them with a premise that no reasoning link feeds into. The link shows 0.36 folded, and 0.72 with the premise set to 100%, against the authors' coarse 90%. On the IABIED map, 0.93 and 0.67 are the same two kinds of numbers for the "If anyone builds it, everyone dies" link.

The ask

Find a step or claim you disagree with and let me know with the "💬 give feedback on this" button in the selected node's popup, or with the "💬 Feedback" button in the full app's toolbar, also anonymously.

Write a small toy example in the editor (full app -> advanced mode -> editor) that shows where the computed number is wrong. The "semantics audit" example group in the map picker shows what an example could look like. Confirmed errors get fixed and credited by name.

And if you find yourself in some discussion about AI risk that is covered by the book, you can link the exact step: "copy link to this" on a node's popup will load the map as you unfolded it and focus that node, and keeps your dragged what-if numbers.

Appendix

Build date

The numbers in this post follow the map's build from 2026-10-15. The maps embedded here follow the live site, so there may be some drift. Changes are documented in the maps' sources with their reasons.

Where the probability goes missing

Reasoning links carry logical structure and only strengthen the conclusion or negated conclusion where they apply. That means that for each claim, in some percentage of cases none of the reasoning links into this claim apply. These cases count as even odds.

On a claim card, the paler top of a gauge is that half share.

In the first example, we have rain at 80% and the link "rain -> street wet" at 90%. The street reads 0.86 (0.8 × 0.95 + 0.2 × one half: the link's 90% is a floor, so where it rains, at least 90 of 100 cases are wet, the rest at even odds; without rain, nothing is said and these cases also count at even odds). Drag the rain down and the paler strip widens. Drag it to 0% and the gauge goes grey (a claim with a single support at zero and nothing arguing against it just shows a grey stripe).

The second example has the inverse link "no rain -> dry" at 90% and the street is 0.77 at rest. The same drag of rain down to 0% puts the street down to 0.05.

On the IABIED map, there is also an example with no inverse link on purpose: "Enormous economic and strategic incentives drive the race", since an ASI could even be built under other motives. Drag it and "What physics permits, someone eventually builds" to 0 and "Anyone builds an ASI" still lands at 0.45 with the even-odds fill.

Arguments do not vote

Let's look at another example to see how multiple reasons for and against a claim interact and why support and objection on the same case don't touch each other if possible.

Below you see two toy examples arguing for a product launch. The first has one support at 85% against one objection at 15%. The second has five supports at 85% against one objection at 15%. In both the launch is at 0.85.

If you drag the objection to 0%, the claim absent the objection reads 0.925 with one support (1 - (1 - 0.85) × half), and 1.00 with five (1 - (1 - 0.85)^5 × half).

(Drag four of five supports to 0% against the objection at 15% and nothing changes, still 0.85.)

Humans often learn well through stories, where long lists of reasons impress themselves into the listener's memory merely through the length of their serialization into language, and where independence structures are rarely more complicated than simple chains or fans. If this example was told as one, it could be very convincing: five inputs all counted as independent 85:15 evidence multiply to (85/15)^5 = about 5,800 to 1. It would then be easy to overlook the single objection (which if multiplied would only multiply 15/85 to cancel one of the five supports, still very convincing at 1,030 to 1).

To fix this, in ArgMap, objections can be beaten by a response, a lower number, or doubt about their premises. So as long as the numbers fit, a multiplicity of supports outvoting them is not enough.

And if there are many supports against many objections, human reasoning about all of them breaks down.

Reasoning links compete only where their grounds hold together

Alice laughed. "There's no use trying," she said: "one can't believe impossible things."

"I daresay you haven't had much practice," said the Queen. "When I was your age, I always did it for half-an-hour a day. Why, sometimes I've believed as many as six impossible things before breakfast."

Lewis Carroll, Through the Looking-Glass

What happens when two (or more) links on the same premise claim more than all of a conclusion's cases?

In this example we see two diary entries that promise too much, 90% for Monday and 70% against Monday, given that the diary is reliable. The diary's reliability itself nobody has vouched for, in the non-conflicting case it sits filled at even odds.

In ArgMap, a for- and against-link resting on the same grounds never apply together and the excess 0.60 (90% + 70% = 160%) cannot happen. The cases producing the contradiction become rarer, and the doubt lands on the diary's reliability that is free to give. It falls from 0.50 to 0.21 and Monday reads 0.55.

Now drag the diary to 100%. It holds and the two links bend instead until they fit, with no excess left. Monday now reads 0.72.

Contrapositively, this gives rise to another authoring rule: If you want to author two links with contradicting conclusions and you want them to not compete with each other, you must put them on different grounds that cannot hold together: by explicitly naming the variable that distinguishes the two.

How firmly each number holds

Under disagreement of the authored numbers something has to give. This was already visible in the diary example above when the diary's reliability was held high.

What gives how much is determined by an additional parameter to links and claims.

Each reasoning link has a kind that is also read from the authors' language: formal, deductive, mechanism, empirical, testimony, analogy, hope.

The currency of these kinds is the number of coin flips at which their link is held when you drag something: formal never bends; deductive 1000; mechanism 64; empirical 16 or an optional sample size; testimony 16; analogy 4; hope 4; default 16. A number of 4 coin flips gives easily and 1000 moves little. The number held at n coin flips resists a change like n observations at that rate would.

Claims with an authors' range give depending on the width of that range: 18 flips for a range of 0.85 to 0.95, 8 for 0.7 to 0.9, 198 for a point interval. More specifically, claims with a width of four points or more give before any mechanism or deductive link.

Prior art

There are already similar systems, each lacking something an author needs:

Markov logic networks have weights instead of probabilities, and the joint distribution is normalized by the partition function over the whole model. A weight's effect depends on every other one and that's why they lack the ability to be elicited locally. ArgMap takes probabilities as inputs and solves for the factor weights.

Probabilistic conditional logic under maximum entropy (Paris 1994; Kern-Isberner 1998, 2001) is a close relative, has authored numbers as a single conditional, solved with a similar projection, but with hard constraints, which needs a consistent knowledge base. Later work (Potyka and Thimm 2014, 2015) handles inconsistency by first minimizing the violation and then choosing among the distributions at the minima, whereas ArgMap has a single weighted objective. In ArgMap, a number's meaning differs (a lower bound on the conditional, forcing some mass on the worlds where the conclusion holds given the premises, and leaving the remainder to be filled; not an exact conditional), it starts from the Bayesian network induced by the map, and how firmly each number holds is elicited from the source. This has an author who is locally honest and globally inconsistent as a legitimate end state, without hiding the glue.

MTAIR (Modeling Transformative AI Risks) is a quantitative model based on numbers from modellers through literature review and engagement with experts. ArgMap reads the numbers from an author's words.

AMTAIR (Automating Transformative AI Risk Modeling, 2025) has LLMs extract argument structure from AI safety papers into an ArgDown-like syntax, probabilities into a "BayesDown" syntax, then a Bayesian network with CPTs and prediction markets for live updates. The numbers come from the literature via the LLM and from markets, where ArgMap reads them from an author's confidence language. The output is a Bayesian network, where ArgMap uses for/against links with argument nesting.

ArgMap is very different from other types of argument mapping like Argdown, Argunet, Kialo (these are almost purely structural) or Concludia (non-probabilistic), and wiki approaches like Arbital (explorable explanations) with its "lenses" as tabs explaining a page at several depths and where users could cast probability votes on claims but which weren't further processed.

This difference is the map filling the cases where nobody builds an ASI with anything like current methods and everyone is killed by one anyway, for example by an ASI built elsewhere or with other methods. The map's link against the claim ("if nobody builds it, it kills nobody", read at 0.9 from the book's words) leaves roughly one in ten cases open, and these cases count at even odds, which contributes (1-0.835) × 0.038 = 0.006.

    Compare Aumann's agreement theorem, where two people with the same prior whose posteriors are common knowledge will arrive at the same posterior. Aumann names "errors in calculating posteriors" as one reason for lasting disagreement. In ArgMap the two are the authors' stated confidence for a claim and the map's computation based on the authors' own numbers in the detailed reasoning. They should agree, and a gap means that one of the calculations is off. But the theorem says nothing about the agreed-upon posterior being right; the two could still be wrong together. So whether the authors' premises are true is for the reader to judge (and adjust in What-if mode!).

Home Alone

The story of our time, told once again: Americans are abandoning quite a lot of formerly popular activities, especially hosting at home, as Derek Thompson discussed. Phones and other electronics are in, most things that are not phones are out, with notably rare exceptions.

That last line rules everything around us. And we all spend more time at home, which then exploded during Covid and mostly did not recover afterward.

Derek does discuss the last two lines later on.

You can view exercise classes as an adaptation in four ways: To a lack of other physical activity, to a lack of social activity, to a lack of motivation, and as a wealth effect. Regular people can afford this, and it is a safe way to get things they now lack.

Then there are the concerts. This one is what some call a Narrative Violation. We have this collective story about how in the good old days, like the 1960s, people went to all these great cheap concerts, that was part of the good life, and we’ve gotten away from that. But actually they’re making a quiet comeback despite people getting older and all the competition, and also they are great. On the flip side, they are also ‘free’ actions, in that you don’t have to overcome any social barrier. You can buy a ticket.

Whereas hosting is, as Derek says, a lot of work to set up, often not fun work. If you’re both working, and children now require vastly more time investment because our society went insane there, who has the time and energy to earn the payoff? Parties also require (and help create and maintain) friends, and creating and maintaining those friends takes even more time.

Meanwhile, being alone at home is no longer boring. Being alone at home is great, in the short term.

Derek Thompson: Machines in the last half century have accomplished something stranger. They have made other people less necessary to our leisure. Every generation has acquired better ways to entertain itself without leaving the house. The result is a peculiar triumph of modern abundance: We have built a world in which being alone has never been easier, more comfortable, or more fun. And then we wonder why everybody stopped coming over.

… Is this what we want? At the risk of invoking Clintonian levels of abstruseness, it depends on what “want” means. Everybody might prefer, in the abstract, a world of dinner parties, neighborhood friendships, and spontaneous gatherings. But on any given Wednesday at 7:45pm., it is easier to look at a screen than to host a party; easier to listen to a podcast while doing yoga than to plan a gathering. This is not so much an individual failure as a coordination failure.

There is some coordination failure, but I think this is the wrong central diagnosis. Coordination failure can be overcome, and given the will to do the thing the logistics are far easier today with all our social and communication and logistical tools.

The bigger problem is hyperbolic discounting in the face of the new alternatives. In order to get the returns from social activity, you have to invest energy and effort now, and also endure some mild social awkwardness and delay gratification and tolerate some boredom now, and often do things for someone else, in order to build up your friendship and other networks and get into regular habits.

I’m also guilty of this trap. I don’t socialize enough. I don’t host enough, and I don’t visit enough. I realize this. But it’s tough. There’s too much to do, both for work and for play. In my case I like to think I have a good excuse, but it is still a mistake.

The Men Have Never Been Okay

Institute for Family Studies reports at length on America’s demoralized and lost men. Their central presentation is not that young men have, as Senator Hawley put it, ‘no vision for what it is to be a man,’ or that their vision would be bad and captured by toxic influences. It’s that they do have such a positive vision, and it would be good but they despair of living up to it and do not see a path to getting there. We no longer lay out a simple ‘success sequence’ style strategy where you play by the rules and it does not work even for those without problems, and many have problems. The men are culturally told that, by default, they are worthless and unwanted.

Or is that the real story? There are some strange sets of beliefs reported.

42% think they are failures and 60% feel they have little control. 72% say who you know is more important than hard work, and 49% saying ‘no matter how hard I work, people like me will never achieve the American dream.’

But 84% say they are at least somewhat ambitious and 81% say they can ‘do just about anything I really set my mind to,’ 75% say their opportunities in life will be greater than their parents, and 82% say they have more potential to succeed than people think.

This seems like a lot of very strong framing effects combined with the Revolution of Rising Expectations. The men believe all these things at the same time, in different ways, and you can ‘activate different personas.’ Connections can beat hard work and the deck is stacked against you, but hard work is valid, and if you want it enough and keep your head on straight and resist temptation and despair you can still succeed. But do you want it enough? Can you keep your head on straight and resist temptation and despair?

And can you keep searching for an unknown, rather than for a known, so long as the ultimate odds have not changed so much?

Another way of looking at this is that if you succeed, there was some way in which you got lucky or did something extraordinary. Something individually atypical is part of every typical success story, even more so than in the past. But if you keep pushing, and try to make your own luck, you will probably eventually get lucky.

There are charts and statistics about the usual suspects, like unemployment, depression, disabilities, games, social media, atomization, gambling and pornography.

Social media is not like the others, where ‘once a day’ is considered infrequent.

Over half of young men feel lonely ‘at least some of the time’ but it is kind of weird not to, isn’t it? The right rate of feeling lonely, like many bad things, is not zero.

The report has many other interesting charts. It would be cool to see time lapses.

Mostly I came away from this report feeling better rather than worse, if you don’t think AI will upend everything. Ways exist to be found, at least for now. Remember that throughout history, a huge percentage of men failed to have children. It is not a new situation for men to be tested and have to find a way to prove themselves.

Broadly my current perspective is the men as a group have never been okay. The difference is that we used to sort of think not being okay was fine. Now we don’t.

A lot of the time, the true argument is of the form ‘there are these weird (and other attributes you or your politics will dislike) people who care about AI safety, but as I’ve shown such people are weird and bad, therefore you shouldn’t care about AI safety.’

Then there are those who accuse the EAs of saying ‘only they can be trusted with AGI’ or that they want to take over the world. Some form of this is narrowly true of the leaders and many employees of the major labs, which includes many EAs at Anthropic, but the same is true of many at OpenAI and Google DeepMind and also Elon Musk, which mostly are not EAs. The active ingredient lies elsewhere.

There is also, yes, a faction that says ‘no one can be trusted, but someone is going to build it and this is our best option,’ the same way that most people are not happy about their choice of Presidential candidate these days. Many are quite upset that Anthropic turned into another race participant, and then there is a split about whether that still makes Anthropic a good enough least-bad option. I believe, in both cases, that those saying ‘you have to pick one’ are making a mistake, but it is similar.

Then there is the larger group of EAs warning that no one can be trusted to build AGI and ASI, period. People are accusing an atheist group of being monotheist because they don’t believe in anyone else’s Gods.

I especially don’t appreciate those who accuse EAs and rationalists of being ‘uniquely isolated’ or ‘ideological’ or attached to their beliefs or anything like that, as in:

Wes (quote is from Sarah Haider): “They tend to hold very binary understanding of emotions and reason, which are, of course, not actually mutually exclusive”

Everyone who views rationalists as caricatures says things like this. Nobody does who has talked to any rationalists for more than 10 minutes.

This is the pure form of the Straw Vulcan style of critique that is remarkably common and has little bearing on reality. Another common one, also available within that thread, is ‘if you follow their logic to its conclusion it implies bad things.’ Yes, if you blindly and endlessly extrapolate from chosen beliefs, in a way that approximately zero people actually do, without pausing to realize your mistake, you eventually get to some rather large mistakes. That is true of everyone who believes something, and also is an important hint about difficulties with AI alignment.

I do think, similarly to Trace Woodgrains, that EAs in particular will often use calculations to imply things that if fully naively extrapolated would go badly, biting bullets in theory, but then in the face of messy reality they wisely pull back in practice. Sometimes things get taken too far, but if there is not a dramatic penalty for too far and you never take things too far then you are not taking things far enough. Note that I explicitly disendorse the strong form of impartiality, among other related bullets.

The classic good faith mistake is to take the ‘in theory’ pronouncements, and then presume people who rhetorically bite those bullets actually fully bite them in practice, or that they would if given the opportunity.

Others, such as the Economist profile, talk about EA as having been ‘led astray.’ Usually it is that they abandoned other causes for AI. In the Economist case it is the better critique that they inadvertently sped AI up in various ways, which is highly valid, I was mad about it at the time, but it cannot be undone. The other critique, about becoming a ‘strict-church’ and encouraging earning to give are less clear, and hopefully few people are still doing classic ‘earning to give’ at this point.

It got bad enough that Tyler Cowen had to go and write In Defense of Effective Altruism. The defense is measured. EA is endorsed on the margin and as directionally correct. As much as Tyler ‘just says things’ regarding AI existential risk, he agrees that obviously we should pay more attention to AI safety, as well as other EA causes like global poverty. Does Tyler have digs and critiques as well? Why yes he does, but to be directionally right on the margin is high praise from a coauthor of Marginal Revolution.
